report.source_text: Considering physical examination, the patient had complete bilateral horizontal gaze palsy in the horizontal plane while vertical gaze was normal, aside from slightly decreased velocity of saccadic movements. Pupils were midsize and reactive, and nystagmus, diplopia or blurry vision were not found. Mild bilateral peripheral facial nerve palsy was also presented in the physical exam. Hyperreflexia in all four limbs was detectable without clonus, plantar reflexes were down going, and muscle forces were not reduced. There were no apparent signs of spasticity and ataxia. All other physical exam findings were normal.

report.source_text: Magnetic resonance imaging indicated multiple hyperintense subcortical, and periventricular lesions visible on the fluid-attenuated inversion recovery (FLAIR) and T2-weighted images, in addition to bilaterally involving PPRF at the level of the pons, anterior to the cerebral aqueduct (Figs. 1-a, b). Two hyperintense lesions were also presented in the sagittal sections of the spinal MRI, one at the level of C7 and the other adjacent to T4. The lesions visible on the MRI were consistent with demyelination. After gadolinium injection, the PPRF lesions were not enhanced, however, T4 thoracic spine lesion was enhanced.

report.source_text: The patient was treated with 1000 mg of intravenous methylprednisolone for three consecutive days, along with other supportive measures. Eye motion indicated significant improvement by passing 1 week from therapy and complete ocular movements were retrieved on the one-month follow up visit of the patient.

clinician.final_diagnosis: diagnosis of MS was made in terms of the 2017 revised McDonald’s criteria
clinician.trajectory_summary: A 16-year-old girl presented with sudden bilateral horizontal gaze palsy, progressive paresthesia in the feet and trunk, and prior similar symptoms. Neurological examination showed bilateral horizontal gaze palsy, mild bilateral peripheral facial nerve palsy, hyperreflexia without weakness or ataxia. Clinical history supported two CNS attacks at distinct sites. MRI revealed multiple hyperintense demyelinating lesions in the brain (subcortical, periventricular, and PPRF of the pons) and spinal cord (C7 and T4), with one active enhancing lesion demonstrating dissemination in time. CSF oligoclonal band analysis was not reported. The patient was treated with corticosteroids and showed significant clinical improvement. This clinical, radiological, and treatment response supports the diagnosis of multiple sclerosis according to the 2017 revised McDonald criteria.
